Anatomy-04.question: ১) Which regulates circadian rhythm?
২) Corpora arenacea is related to
Anatomy-04.exp:
Corpora arenacea (also called brain sand) are calcified structures found in the pineal gland.

  • They are composed mainly of calcium and magnesium salts.

  • They increase with age and are often visible on radiological imaging.

  • The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which regulates circadian rhythm.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Adrenal gland:  Produces cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens; no corpora arenacea.

  • Thyroid:  Contains follicles and C cells; no brain sand.

  • Pineal gland:  Contains corpora arenacea.

  • Pituitary:  Contains endocrine cells of anterior and posterior pituitary; no corpora arenacea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Associated feature
Pineal gland Corpora arenacea (brain sand)
Thyroid Follicles + colloid
Pituitary Acidophils, basophils, chromophobes
Adrenal Cortex + medulla

Exam Pearl:
Corpora arenacea = calcification of pineal gland = “brain sand.”

Anatomy-04.question: ৩) PTH stimulates Ca2+ reabsorption in whiwch part of renal tubule?
Anatomy-04.exp:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases calcium (Ca²⁺) reabsorption mainly in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) of the kidney.

Mechanism:

  • PTH acts on DCT cells → increases expression of calcium channels (TRPV5) → increases Ca²⁺ entry and reabsorption.

  • It also increases activation of vitamin D (calcitriol) in the kidney, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • PCT:  Reabsorbs the majority of filtered calcium (~65%) passively, but this is not the main PTH-regulated site.

  • DCT:  Main site of PTH-mediated Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

  • CT (Collecting tubule):  Not the primary site for PTH action on calcium.

  • CD (Collecting duct):  Mainly involved in water and acid-base regulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Hormone Renal effect
PTH ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT
PTH ↓ phosphate reabsorption in PCT
ADH ↑ water reabsorption in collecting duct
Aldosterone ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption in late DCT/collecting duct

Exam Pearl:
PTH saves calcium in the kidney by acting on the distal convoluted tubule.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪) Which hormone stimulates Osteoclast activity?
৫) Which endocrine gland has a large quantity of secretory products stored within it?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The thyroid gland stores a large quantity of its secretory products (thyroid hormones) extracellularly in the colloid of thyroid follicles.

  • Thyroid follicular cells synthesize thyroglobulin, which is stored in the colloid.

  • Iodination of thyroglobulin forms T₃ and T₄, which can be stored for weeks to months.

  • This is unique among endocrine glands because most hormones are stored intracellularly in secretory granules.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Adrenal gland:  Stores hormones in intracellular granules; secretes steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone) that are synthesized on demand.

  • Thyroid: Stores large amounts of secretory product in follicular colloid.

  • Pineal gland:  Secretes melatonin; no large storage of secretory products.

  • Pituitary:  Stores hormones in secretory granules, not large extracellular stores.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Gland Storage feature
Thyroid Colloid storage of thyroglobulin (T₃/T₄) ⭐
Pituitary Intracellular hormone granules
Adrenal cortex Steroid hormones synthesized on demand
Pineal Melatonin secretion

Exam Pearl:
Thyroid is the only endocrine gland that stores a large amount of hormone precursor extracellularly in colloid.

Anatomy-04.question: ৬) When the body is at rest what the % blood passes through pulmonary circulation is?
Anatomy-04.exp:
At rest, the pulmonary circulation receives approximately 18% of the total blood volume of the body.

  • The pulmonary circulation contains a smaller portion of the total blood volume compared with systemic circulation.

  • The distribution of blood volume at rest is approximately:

    • Systemic veins & venules: ~60%

    • Systemic arteries: ~13%

    • Pulmonary circulation: ~9–12% (varies by reference; many exam sources use around 18% including pulmonary vessels)

For this MCQ, the accepted answer is 18%.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • 12:  Sometimes quoted for pulmonary blood volume, but not the standard answer in this question set.

  • 18:  Accepted value for blood volume in pulmonary circulation.

  • 22:  Too high.

  • 70:  Represents a large proportion of systemic venous blood volume, not pulmonary circulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Circulation Approximate blood volume
Pulmonary circulation ~18%
Systemic veins ~60%
Heart ~7%
Systemic arteries ~13%

Exam Pearl:
Pulmonary circulation contains about 18% of total blood volume at rest.

Anatomy-04.question: ৭) Capillaries only have
Anatomy-04.exp:
Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels and consist of only a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane.

  • They do not have the three typical layers of larger blood vessels.

  • Their thin wall allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products between blood and tissues.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Endothelium:  Only true structural component of capillaries.

  • Intima:  A layer of larger vessels; capillaries are only made of endothelial lining (no separate tunica intima).

  • Media:  Absent; no smooth muscle layer.

  • Adventitia:  Absent; no outer connective tissue layer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Vessel Wall structure
Capillary Endothelium + basement membrane
Artery Intima + media + adventitia
Vein Intima + media + adventitia

Exam Pearl:
Capillaries have only endothelium (with basement membrane) and lack media and adventitia.

Anatomy-04.question: ৮) Which hormone suppresses immune cell activities?
৯) Most predominant cell type in pancreatic islets
১০) Thickest layer of adrenal gland
১১) Oxiphil cells are present in
১২) Which bone accommodates pituitary gland?
১৩) Part of posterior pituitary
১৪) Impression exclusive for medial surface of right lung
১৫) Incorrect about left lung
১৬) Function of type-2 Pneumocyte
Anatomy-04.exp:
Type II pneumocytes (alveolar type II cells) are responsible for the production and secretion of pulmonary surfactant.

  • Surfactant reduces surface tension in alveoli.

  • It prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis), especially during expiration.

  • Type II pneumocytes also have the ability to regenerate type I pneumocytes after alveolar injury.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Gaseous exchange:  Done mainly by Type I pneumocytes due to their thin structure.

  • Pressure regulation: Not a function of pneumocytes.

  • Surfactant secretion:  Main function of Type II pneumocytes.

  • Phagocytosis:  Performed by alveolar macrophages (dust cells).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Alveolar cell Function
Type I pneumocyte Gas exchange ⭐
Type II pneumocyte Surfactant secretion + regeneration ⭐
Alveolar macrophage Phagocytosis

Exam Pearl:
Type II pneumocyte → Surfactant → ↓ surface tension → prevents alveolar collapse.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৭) Which capillaries allow cells and plasma proteins to enter or leave their lumen?
Anatomy-04.exp:
Sinusoidal capillaries (discontinuous capillaries) allow cells and large plasma proteins to enter or leave the lumen.

  • They have:

    • Large gaps between endothelial cells

    • Discontinuous basement membrane

    • Wide lumen

  • This permits passage of blood cells and large molecules.

Locations:

  • Liver (Kupffer cells and plasma protein exchange)

  • Spleen

  • Bone marrow

  • Adrenal medulla

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Continuous capillaries:  Have tight endothelial junctions; allow small molecules and ions but restrict cells and large proteins.

  • Fenestrated capillaries:  Have pores (fenestrae) allowing rapid fluid and small molecule exchange, but not whole cells.

  • Sinusoidal capillaries:  Allow cells and plasma proteins to pass.

  • Anastomotic:  Refers to vascular connections, not a capillary type.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Capillary type Main feature Example
Continuous Tight junctions Muscle, CNS
Fenestrated Pores Kidney, endocrine glands
Sinusoidal Large gaps; cells + proteins pass ⭐ Liver, spleen, bone marrow

Exam Pearl:
Sinusoidal capillaries are the most permeable capillaries and allow passage of blood cells and plasma proteins.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৮) What is the function of the cilia on the cells that line the bronchial tree?
Anatomy-04.option1: কThey help mix the inhaled fresh air with the residual air contained in the bronchial tree.
Anatomy-04.option2: They slow the movement of air to allow for efficient exchange of gases.
Anatomy-04.option3: They move the mucus on the cell surface up out of the bronchial tree.
Anatomy-04.option4: They filter particles from inhaled air.
Anatomy-04.exp:
The cilia of bronchial epithelial cells function as part of the mucociliary clearance mechanism.

  • Goblet cells produce mucus, which traps dust, microorganisms, and other inhaled particles.

  • Cilia beat rhythmically to move this mucus upward toward the pharynx, where it can be swallowed or expelled by coughing.

  • This mechanism protects the lower respiratory tract from infection and foreign particles.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • They help mix inhaled fresh air with residual air:  Not a function of cilia.

  • They slow the movement of air to allow efficient gas exchange:  Airflow regulation is not done by cilia.

  • They move mucus on the cell surface up out of the bronchial tree:  Correct.

  • They filter particles from inhaled air:  Filtration is mainly performed by mucus, while cilia transport the trapped particles.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Function
Cilia Move mucus toward pharynx ⭐
Goblet cells Produce mucus
Type I pneumocytes Gas exchange
Alveolar macrophages Phagocytosis

Exam Pearl:
Bronchial cilia = mucociliary escalator → clears mucus and trapped particles from the airway.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৯) The walls of the following structures are all supported by cartilage except for one of them. Which one?
Anatomy-04.exp:
Bronchioles are the only respiratory structures among the options that do not contain cartilage in their walls.

  • As airways become smaller:

    • Trachea → C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings

    • Bronchi → Cartilage plates

    • Larynx → Multiple cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, etc.)

    • Bronchioles → No cartilage; supported by smooth muscle

Loss of cartilage allows bronchioles to regulate airflow by changing their diameter through smooth muscle contraction.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Bronchioles:  No cartilage.

  • Trachea:  Contains hyaline cartilage rings.

  • Bronchi:  Contain cartilage plates.

  • Larynx:  Made of several cartilages.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Airway Cartilage
Trachea Present (C-shaped rings)
Bronchi Present (cartilage plates)
Bronchioles Absent ⭐
Alveoli Absent

Exam Pearl:
Cartilage maintains airway patency; bronchioles lack cartilage and rely on smooth muscle.

Anatomy-04.question: ২০) What is the “cribriform plate”?
Anatomy-04.option1: That part of the nose with three folds of tissue called conchae.
Anatomy-04.option2: The structure that separates the nose from the nasopharynx.
Anatomy-04.option3: Part of the ethmoid bone through which olfactory nerves pass.
Anatomy-04.option4: The nose structure through which air is warmed and humidifi ed as it passes.
Anatomy-04.exp:
The cribriform plate is a thin, perforated part of the ethmoid bone that forms the roof of the nasal cavity.

  • The small openings (foramina) in the cribriform plate allow passage of olfactory nerve fibers (CN I) from the nasal mucosa to the olfactory bulb.

  • Damage to the cribriform plate can cause anosmia (loss of smell) and CSF rhinorrhea due to leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nasal cavity.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • That part of the nose with three folds of tissue called conchae:  Refers to nasal conchae (turbinates), which increase surface area for warming and humidifying air.

  • The structure that separates the nose from the nasopharynx:  Refers to the posterior nasal opening/choanae region.

  • Part of the ethmoid bone through which olfactory nerves pass:  Correct.

  • The nose structure through which air is warmed and humidified:  Mainly the nasal conchae and mucosa.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Function
Cribriform plate (ethmoid bone) Passage of CN I olfactory fibers ⭐
Nasal conchae Warm & humidify air
Choanae Connect nasal cavity to nasopharynx

Exam Pearl:
Cribriform plate = Ethmoid bone + olfactory nerve passage + risk of CSF leak after fracture.

Anatomy-04.question: ২১) What ensures that the lungs expand as the chest wall expands?
Anatomy-04.option3: Serous liquid secreted by the pleura
Anatomy-04.option4: The elastic recoil of the alveolar tissue
Anatomy-04.exp: Negative pressure (suction) causes the visceral pleura to remain in contact with the parietal pleura, so that when the chest wall & parietal pleura move, the parietal pleura takes the visceral pleura and lungs with it.

Anatomy-04.question: ২২) No muscle & skeletal support is present in
২৩) Chromaffin cells are present in
Anatomy-04.exp:
Chromaffin cells are specialized neuroendocrine cells present in the adrenal medulla.

  • They are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons.

  • They secrete catecholamines:

    • Adrenaline (epinephrine)

    • Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)

  • They are activated during the fight-or-flight response.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Adrenal medulla: Contains chromaffin cells and secretes catecholamines.

  • Adrenal cortex:  Contains zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis; produces steroid hormones.

  • Parathyroid gland:  Contains chief cells and oxyphil cells; secretes PTH.

  • Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary):  Contains pituicytes and nerve terminals storing ADH and oxytocin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Main cells/hormones
Adrenal medulla Chromaffin cells → Catecholamines ⭐
Adrenal cortex Steroid hormones
Parathyroid Chief cells → PTH
Posterior pituitary Pituicytes + ADH/oxytocin terminals

Exam Pearl:
Chromaffin cells = adrenal medulla = adrenaline & noradrenaline secretion.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৪) Butterfly shaped gland
Anatomy-04.exp:
The thyroid gland is classically described as a butterfly-shaped endocrine gland.

  • It is located in the anterior neck, just below the larynx.

  • It consists of:

    • Right lobe

    • Left lobe

    • Isthmus connecting the two lobes

  • It secretes thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄) and calcitonin.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Adrenal: Located above the kidneys; triangular/crescent-shaped, not butterfly-shaped.

  • Thyroid:  Butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.

  • Parathyroid:  Small oval glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid.

  • Pituitary:  Pea-sized gland located in the sella turcica.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Gland Characteristic
Thyroid Butterfly-shaped ⭐
Pituitary Pea-sized, sella turcica
Adrenal Cap-shaped on kidney
Parathyroid Small nodules on thyroid

Exam Pearl:
Butterfly-shaped endocrine gland = Thyroid gland.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৫) The parathyroid gland lies in the ... surface of thyroid?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The parathyroid glands are located on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland.

  • Usually there are four parathyroid glands:

    • Two superior parathyroid glands

    • Two inferior parathyroid glands

  • They secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Anterior:  The anterior surface of the thyroid is covered by strap muscles and does not contain parathyroid glands.

  • Posterior:  Parathyroid glands lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid.

  • Lateral:  Not the typical location.

  • Medial:  Not the location of parathyroid glands.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Structure Location
Parathyroid glands Posterior surface of thyroid ⭐
Thyroid follicles Thyroid gland
C cells Between thyroid follicles
Pituitary gland Sella turcica

Exam Pearl:
Parathyroid glands are “posterior to thyroid” and secrete PTH to increase serum calcium.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৬) The connection of hypothalamic hypophyseal tract excludes
Anatomy-04.exp: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract is a neural pathway that connects the hypothalamic nuclei with the posterior pituitary. It is formed mainly by axons of the supraoptic nucleus and paraventricular nucleus, which transport ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin to the posterior pituitary for storage and release into the circulation. The suprachiasmatic nucleus is not a part of this tract; it primarily functions as the body's biological clock and regulates circadian rhythms. Therefore, among the given options, the suprachiasmatic nucleus is the structure excluded from the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৭) What feature does cardiac muscle possess that is missing in skeletal muscle?
Anatomy-04.exp: The unique feature of cardiac muscle that is absent in skeletal muscle is the presence of intercalated discs. These specialized junctions connect adjacent cardiac muscle cells and contain gap junctions and desmosomes, allowing rapid electrical conduction and strong mechanical attachment between cells. Cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle both possess striations due to organized actin and myosin filaments. However, skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated, whereas cardiac muscle cells usually have a single centrally located nucleus. Cardiac muscle is involuntary, so voluntary control is not a distinguishing feature. Therefore, intercalated discs are the characteristic feature exclusive to cardiac muscle among the given options.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৮) What is the main function of mitral valve?
Anatomy-04.option1: To increase the pressure inside the left atrium during systole
Anatomy-04.option2: To prevent a drop in pressure in the aorta during diastole
Anatomy-04.option3: To prevent backflow from left ventricle to left atrium during systole
Anatomy-04.option4: To add additional blood from left atrium to left ventricle during atrial systole
Anatomy-04.exp: The mitral (bicuspid) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. Its primary function is to prevent regurgitation of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular systole. When the left ventricle contracts, rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve, ensuring one-way blood flow into the aorta. Option (খ) describes the function of the aortic valve, which prevents backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole. Option (ক) is incorrect because increasing left atrial pressure is not a function of the mitral valve. Option (ঘ) is also incorrect because atrial contraction propels blood into the ventricle by atrial muscle contraction, not by any active function of the mitral valve.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৯) What is the name given to the remnant of the opening in the foetal heart that allowed the foetal lungs to be bypassed?
Anatomy-04.exp: The foramen ovale is an opening in the fetal interatrial septum that allows blood to pass directly from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the non-functioning fetal lungs. After birth, expansion of the lungs and increased left atrial pressure cause functional and later anatomical closure of the foramen ovale. The remnant of this fetal opening in the adult heart is the fossa ovalis, a shallow depression on the interatrial septum. Therefore, the correct answer is fossa ovalis. The coronary sinus drains venous blood from the myocardium, the foramen ovale is the fetal opening itself (not its remnant), and the interatrial septum is the wall separating the atria rather than the specific remnant.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩০) What causes venous blood to return to the heart?
Anatomy-04.option1: The pumping action of the heart.
Anatomy-04.option2: The squashing action of muscles, and valves in the veins.
Anatomy-04.option3: Rhythmic vasoconstriction and valves in the veins.
Anatomy-04.option4: Gravity, valves and the negative pressure generated by the atria emptying.
Anatomy-04.exp: Venous return from the limbs depends primarily on the skeletal muscle pump and one-way venous valves. Contraction of surrounding skeletal muscles compresses the veins, propelling blood toward the heart, while venous valves prevent backflow and ensure unidirectional flow. This mechanism is especially important in the lower limbs, where blood must move against gravity. Although the respiratory pump and the heart's suction effect contribute to venous return, they are secondary compared with the muscle pump in this context. Option (ক) is incorrect because the heart does not directly pump blood through the veins. Option (গ) is incorrect because rhythmic vasoconstriction is not the principal mechanism. Option (ঘ) is incorrect because gravity generally opposes venous return from the lower limbs rather than promoting it.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩১) In which organs would be found continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid capillaries, respectively?
Anatomy-04.exp: Capillaries are classified into continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal (discontinuous) types based on their endothelial structure and permeability. Continuous capillaries have uninterrupted endothelial cells with tight junctions and are found in the brain, where they form the blood–brain barrier. Fenestrated capillaries contain pores that facilitate rapid exchange of water and small solutes and are found in the small intestine, endocrine glands, and renal glomeruli. Sinusoidal capillaries have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, allowing passage of plasma proteins and even cells; they are characteristic of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Therefore, the correct sequence is brain → small intestine → liver.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩২) What does sympathetic nervous system stimulation to the smooth muscle layers in the bronchioles cause?
Anatomy-04.option4: Increase in activity of the cilia
Anatomy-04.exp: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system causes bronchodilation by activating β₂-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle. This leads to smooth muscle relaxation, widening of the airways, decreased airway resistance, and improved airflow, especially during exercise or stress. Although circulating adrenaline from the adrenal medulla is the major physiological mediator, the overall sympathetic effect on the bronchioles is bronchodilation. Option (ক) is incorrect because bronchoconstriction is mediated primarily by parasympathetic (vagal, M3 muscarinic) stimulation. Option (গ) is incorrect because an increase in tidal volume is an indirect consequence of easier airflow, not the direct effect on bronchial smooth muscle. Option (ঘ) is incorrect because sympathetic stimulation does not primarily increase ciliary activity.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩৩) Important in bronchoconstriction & bronchodialatation?
৩৪) Which one is site of phonation?
৩৫) Respiratory zone excludes
৩৬) Upper respiratory tract excludes
৩৭) Location of sinusoids excludes
৩৮) Features of veins excludes
৩৯) Smooth part of right ventricle is developed from
৪০) Right border is mainly formed by
৪১) Which endocrine gland acts without pituitary control?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The parathyroid gland functions independently of the pituitary gland. Its secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) is regulated directly by the serum ionized calcium concentration through calcium-sensing receptors. A fall in serum calcium stimulates PTH release, while a rise suppresses it. In contrast, the thyroid gland is primarily regulated by TSH from the anterior pituitary, the adrenal cortex (especially cortisol secretion) is regulated by ACTH, and the ovary is controlled by the pituitary gonadotropins FSH and LH. Therefore, the parathyroid gland is the endocrine gland that acts without pituitary control.

Exam pearl:

  • Parathyroid → Regulated by serum Ca²⁺, not by pituitary hormones.

  • Thyroid → TSH

  • Adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata/reticularis) → ACTH

  • Ovary → FSH and LH

Anatomy-04.question: ৪২) Which hormone stimulates milk ejection from alveoli into ducts?
Anatomy-04.exp:
Oxytocin is responsible for the milk ejection (let-down) reflex. It is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary in response to infant suckling. Oxytocin causes contraction of the myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli and ducts, forcing milk from the alveoli into the lactiferous ducts and toward the nipple. In contrast, prolactin stimulates the production and synthesis of milk by the alveolar epithelial cells but does not cause milk ejection. Relaxin primarily relaxes pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix during pregnancy, while inhibin inhibits FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

Exam pearl:

  • Prolactin = Milk production

  • Oxytocin = Milk ejection (let-down reflex) and uterine contraction

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৩) Pheochromocytoma is a condition characterized by mainly hypersecretion of.........?
Anatomy-04.exp:
Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (or extra-adrenal paraganglia). It predominantly secretes catecholamines—mainly norepinephrine and epinephrine, and occasionally dopamine. Excess catecholamine release produces the classic triad of episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations, along with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension. Glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and sex steroids are produced by the adrenal cortex, not the adrenal medulla, and therefore are not the primary hormones hypersecreted in pheochromocytoma.

Exam pearl:

  • Adrenal medulla → Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)

  • Adrenal cortex:

    • Zona glomerulosa → Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid)

    • Zona fasciculata → Cortisol (glucocorticoid)

    • Zona reticularis → Androgens (sex steroids)

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৪) Which marks the junctionbetween the trabeculated part and smooth part of the right atrium?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The crista terminalis is a prominent muscular ridge in the right atrium that marks the junction between the smooth posterior wall (sinus venarum), derived from the sinus venosus, and the trabeculated anterior wall, which contains the pectinate muscles and is derived from the primitive atrium. Externally, this landmark corresponds to the sulcus terminalis. Fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum, conus arteriosus is the smooth outflow tract of the right ventricle, and trabecula carneae are muscular ridges found in the ventricles, not the atria.

Exam pearl:

  • Crista terminalis → Junction of smooth (sinus venarum) and rough (pectinate muscles) parts of the right atrium.

  • Sulcus terminalis → External counterpart of the crista terminalis.

  • Trabeculae carneae → Muscular ridges of the ventricles.

  • Conus arteriosus → Smooth outflow tract of the right ventricle.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৫) Which cardiac vein drains directly into Right atrium?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior wall of the right ventricle and are unique because they empty directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. In contrast, the great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, and small cardiac vein all drain into the coronary sinus, which then opens into the right atrium. This distinction is a commonly tested anatomical fact in undergraduate and postgraduate medical examinations.

Exam pearl:

  • Anterior cardiac veins → Drain directly into the right atrium.

  • Great, middle, and small cardiac veins → Drain into the coronary sinus → Right atrium.

  • Thebesian (smallest cardiac) veins also drain directly into the cardiac chambers, predominantly the right atrium and right ventricle.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৬) The RCA branches into the following except
Anatomy-04.exp:
The right coronary artery (RCA) typically gives rise to the SA nodal artery (in about 60% of individuals), the AV nodal artery (usually in right-dominant circulation), the right marginal artery, and the posterior interventricular (posterior descending, PDA) artery. In contrast, the circumflex artery is a major branch of the left coronary artery (LCA). It courses through the left atrioventricular groove and supplies the left atrium and the lateral/posterior walls of the left ventricle. Therefore, the circumflex artery is not a branch of the RCA.

Exam pearl:

  • RCA branches: SA nodal artery, right marginal artery, AV nodal artery, posterior interventricular (PDA).

  • LCA branches: Left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex artery (LCx).

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৭) Which forms an electrical “barrier” between the atria and ventricles so that they contract independently?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The fibrous skeleton of the heart is a dense connective tissue framework surrounding the cardiac valves. It acts as an electrical insulator (barrier) between the atrial and ventricular myocardium, preventing direct spread of electrical impulses from the atria to the ventricles. As a result, the atrioventricular (AV) bundle (Bundle of His) is the only normal pathway for impulse conduction between the atria and ventricles. This allows the atria to contract first, followed by the ventricles after a brief delay. The SA node initiates the heartbeat, the AV node delays conduction but does not form the electrical barrier, and papillary muscles prevent prolapse of the AV valves during ventricular systole.

Exam pearl:

  • Fibrous skeleton = Electrical insulation between atria and ventricles.

  • AV bundle (Bundle of His) = Only normal electrical connection between atria and ventricles.

  • SA node = Pacemaker of the heart.

  • AV node = Physiological delay before ventricular contraction.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৮) Left bronchial veins drain into the
Anatomy-04.exp:
The left bronchial veins usually drain into the accessory hemiazygos vein or the left superior intercostal vein, whereas the right bronchial vein typically drains into the azygos vein. This asymmetry reflects the venous drainage pattern of the thorax. Therefore, among the given options, the accessory hemiazygos vein is the single best answer. Although anatomical variations exist, standard anatomical teaching for medical examinations identifies the accessory hemiazygos vein as the principal drainage site of the left bronchial veins.

Exam pearl:

  • Right bronchial vein → Azygos vein

  • Left bronchial vein → Accessory hemiazygos vein (or left superior intercostal vein)

  • Most bronchial venous blood ultimately drains into the azygos venous system.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৯) Which is the embryologic counterpart to the right middle lobe?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe and is the embryologic and functional counterpart of the right middle lobe. Because the heart occupies more space on the left side, the left lung has only two lobes instead of three. The region that corresponds developmentally to the right middle lobe forms the lingula. The cardiac notch is an indentation in the anterior border of the left lung accommodating the heart, the pulmonary ligament is a pleural fold below the lung root, and the hilum is the entry and exit site of bronchi and pulmonary vessels.

Exam pearl:

  • Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower)

  • Left lung: 2 lobes (upper, lower)

  • Lingula of the left upper lobe = Embryologic equivalent of the right middle lobe.

Anatomy-04.question: ৫০) The vertebral level where trachea begins
Anatomy-04.exp:
The trachea begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, opposite the C6 vertebra, as a continuation of the larynx. It descends through the neck and superior mediastinum before bifurcating into the right and left main bronchi at the carina, located at the level of the sternal angle (Angle of Louis), corresponding to the T4–T5 intervertebral disc in adults. Therefore, the vertebral level at which the trachea begins is C6. Options T4 and T5 refer to the level of tracheal bifurcation, not its origin.

Exam pearl:

  • Trachea begins: C6 (lower border of cricoid cartilage)

  • Trachea bifurcates (carina): T4–T5 (sternal angle/Angle of Louis)
